### Observed differences

- Resource allocation shifted across every activity with assignment evidence (A01, A03, A10, A13/A14, A17, A22). In the earlier window, one consistent group of resources held the largest shares — for example User_19 took roughly 5–8 in 100 assignments on six of the seven activities. In the later window that group had fallen to negligible shares (drops of roughly 5–8 in 100 each), while a different group took over — for example User_37 and User_61 rose from absent or marginal to about 4–13 in 100 each; the pooled remainder stayed near half of assignments in both windows, so this is a swap among named resources rather than a dissolve into an anonymous pool. All seven items point the same way, each difference is larger than in all but about 1 in 2000 random re-splits, and the profiles rest on roughly 120–290 assignments per activity per window; A13 and A14 show identical profiles and likely reflect the same events, so they are not independent confirmations. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- Validation de-concentrated. In the earlier window, ten named resources together carried about 91 in 100 of A10 assignments, the largest taking about 19 in 100. In the later window those resources kept only small shares (the largest about 7 in 100, ten named together about 43 in 100), while the pooled remainder of many resources rose from about 9 in 100 to about 57 in 100. [ASSIGN003]
- Activity volumes changed little: the number of observations behind each profile is similar across windows (for example 200 vs 200 for A01, 286 vs 263 for A13, 126 vs 114 for A22), so the shift lies in who executed the activities rather than in how often they ran. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN007]
- One control-flow signal: the gap, in event positions, between consecutive A17 events in the same trace shifted toward smaller gaps — in the later window about 39 in 100 pairs were immediately consecutive versus about 23 in 100 before, while pairs five positions apart fell from about 43 in 100 to about 20 in 100. This rests on only 46 pairs before and 32 after, and is larger than in about 199 of 200 random re-splits. [LAG001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a specific hypothesis about resource allocation: in the later window, execution of the main offer and application activities (A01, A03, A10, A13/A14, A17, A22) moved from the group of resources that dominated the earlier window (for example User_19) to a different group (for example User_37 and User_61), and A10 additionally spread from a small set of resources carrying about 91 in 100 of its assignments to a broad pool carrying about 57 in 100. The resource family produced 7 qualifying items where about 0.005 would be expected without a change; all seven agree in direction (the same resources rising across activities, the same ones falling), each is individually more extreme than all but about 1 in 2000 random re-splits, and each profile rests on roughly 120–290 observations per window, so the pattern is unlikely to be a sampling artefact. The resource codes are anonymous, so a re-labelling of resources cannot be distinguished from a genuine reallocation, and a shift in the mix of cases towards resources that already handled them could produce a similar signature; the evidence cannot rule this out. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

Other differences: a single control-flow item shows the position gap between consecutive A17 events redistributing toward smaller gaps; its family produced 1 item where about 0.2 are expected without a change — what a stable process typically produces — and it rests on only 46 versus 32 pairs, so it does not add support to the hypothesis. No time items qualified. [LAG001]
